title: SafeSteps Nervous System and Regulation Course
subtitle: 12 complete video-first parent lessons, worksheets, quizzes, scenarios and action plans
clinical_notes: Educational content only; not a diagnostic or treatment service.
The three-system brain model and window of tolerance are teaching metaphors, not diagnostic tests.
Fight, flight and freeze are common threat-response shorthand. Fawn/appease is presented as trauma-informed descriptive language, not a formal diagnosis.
Grounding and body-based practices should be optional, gentle and adapted. Stop if they increase distress or physical symptoms.

lessons.title: What Is the Nervous System and Why Does It Matter for Parenting?
lessons.overview: The nervous system is the body's communication, protection and regulation network. It helps a parent notice what is happening, interpret whether something feels safe or threatening, mobilise a response and recover. Parenting under stress can become automatic; learning to notice body activation creates more opportunity to pause and choose a safer response.
objectives: describe the nervous system in plain language
identify how stress changes attention, breathing, muscle tension and behaviour
explain why a parent's body state can influence parenting decisions
notice at least three personal signs of activation
choose one brief pause strategy to practise
lessons.definition_prompt: Before watching the video, what do you believe the nervous system is, and how might it affect the way a parent responds to a child?
checkin: I notice body changes before I become angry, frightened or overwhelmed.
I sometimes react before I have fully understood what is happening.
When I am stressed, I may speak faster, louder or more sharply.
I can usually pause long enough to choose my response.
I know at least one safe way to help my body settle.
key_points: A communication network
The brain, spinal cord and nerves continually exchange information with the body and environment.
A protection system
The body can rapidly mobilise energy and attention when it detects possible danger or intense stress.
A regulation system
The nervous system also supports recovery, rest, digestion, connection and flexible thinking.
Why parenting is affected
Stress can narrow attention and make behaviour look more threatening, deliberate or urgent than it is.
The practical goal
The goal is not permanent calm. It is earlier awareness, safer choices and more reliable repair.

video_scenes: Soft animated network linking brain, spinal cord, heart, lungs, stomach and muscles.
Your nervous system is a communication and safety network. It links your brain, body, senses, emotions and actions. Much of its work happens automatically, before you have time to think about it.
Your nervous system: notice - interpret - respond - recover
Parent preparing dinner. Child repeatedly calls out and knocks over a cup. Subtle visual overlays show faster heartbeat and tight shoulders.

Imagine you are already tired and rushed. A cup spills and your child shouts. Your nervous system may register noise, mess and loss of control as urgent. Your heart may speed up, your jaw may tighten and your attention may narrow.
Stress changes the body
First version: parent points, raises voice and says, 'Why do you always do this?' Child recoils and begins crying.
When the body is highly activated, a parent can move into an automatic response. The parent may assume the child was careless on purpose, use a harsh voice or act before gathering information.
Automatic reaction
Rewind effect. Second version pauses at the tight-jaw moment. Parent puts both feet down, exhales, looks at the spill and lowers shoulders.

Now watch the same moment with one small pause. The parent notices, 'My shoulders are tight and I want to yell.' They place both feet on the floor and make the out-breath a little longer. The problem has not disappeared, but there is more room to choose.
Notice - pause - choose
Parent says calmly, 'The cup spilled. Step back so no one slips. I will get a towel and you can help.' Child settles and helps.
A regulated response can still include a clear limit. Calm does not mean permissive. The parent protects safety, gives a simple instruction and involves the child in repair without shame.
Calm and firm can happen together
Split screen: left shows tight body/rapid speech; right shows slower movement and neutral expression. Child's body state mirrors each version.

Children read adult tone, posture, facial expression and pace. A parent's nervous system does not control a child's feelings, but it can either add threat or offer signals of safety and predictability.
Body states affect interaction
Simple four-step graphic and parent later writing a plan card.

The first skill is not to force yourself to feel calm. It is to notice activation earlier. Ask: What is happening in my body? Is anyone in immediate danger? What pause can I safely create? What response protects both safety and connection?
1 Notice  2 Check safety  3 Pause  4 Respond

This week, practise noticing one body signal before you respond. Small pauses, repeated over time, can increase choice.
Earlier notice creates more choice

options: Attention may narrow and behaviour may seem more threatening

lessons.title: Your Brain in Three Parts - Survival, Emotional and Thinking
lessons.overview: This lesson uses a simplified three-system teaching model: protective/survival processes, emotional/relational processes and thinking/planning processes. These are not three separate brains; they are overlapping networks used as a practical way to understand why clear thinking becomes harder under stress.
objectives: use the three-system model without treating it as literal anatomy
recognise protective, emotional and thinking responses in parenting
identify what makes flexible thinking less available
practise moving from alarm toward choice
use language that reduces shame and increases responsibility
lessons.definition_prompt: What do the words survival brain, emotional brain and thinking brain mean to you? How do you think they work together during conflict?
checkin: When I feel threatened or disrespected, I focus on stopping the behaviour immediately.
Strong feelings can make it hard for me to listen or problem-solve.
I can sometimes name my feelings without acting on them.
I find it easier to think after my body has settled.
I can hold a boundary while remaining curious about what my child needs.
key_points: A teaching model, not literal anatomy
The brain works through connected networks. The three-system model is a simplified way to organise protective, emotional and thinking functions.
Protective or survival processes
Rapidly scan for danger and prepare the body to act, escape, become still or seek safety.
Emotional and relational processes
Add feelings, memories, attachment needs and social meaning to what is happening.
Thinking and planning processes
Support attention, inhibition, perspective, language, problem-solving and future consequences.
Integration
Safer parenting is more likely when the parent can notice protection and emotion while bringing thinking back online.
lessons.video_goal: Use an animated traffic-light brain metaphor and a parent-child bedtime conflict to show how the three systems overlap.
video_scenes: Animated brain made of overlapping translucent networks, not separate stacked sections.

People often hear that the brain has a survival part, an emotional part and a thinking part. This is a useful teaching model, but the brain is not literally three separate brains. These functions overlap and communicate.
A simplified three-system model
Protective network highlights as a smoke alarm icon appears.

Protective processes act like a fast alarm. They scan for possible danger and prepare the body to respond. They are essential for safety, but they can also activate during conflict, noise, rejection, embarrassment or memories of earlier experiences.
Protective: fast safety response
Emotional network highlights with memory snapshots and connection icons.
Emotional and relational processes add feelings, memories and meaning. A child's refusal may connect with a parent's fear of losing control, not being respected or failing as a parent.
Emotional: feelings, memory, connection
Thinking network highlights with speech bubble, plan and pause icons.

Thinking and planning processes help us slow down, use words, consider another person's perspective, remember goals and predict consequences. These abilities become harder to access when stress is very high.
Thinking: pause, plan, perspective
Bedtime scene. Child says, 'I'm not going to bed.' Parent's protection system labels it 'challenge'; emotional system adds 'I am being ignored.' Parent begins lecturing.

At bedtime, a child refuses. The protective system may hear a challenge. The emotional system may add, 'No one respects me.' If activation rises, the thinking system has less room to ask whether the child is anxious, overtired, seeking connection or testing a routine.
Stress can reduce flexible thinking
Rewind. Parent labels systems: 'Alarm is high. I feel rejected. My goal is a safe bedtime.' Parent gives two choices.

The parent can name what is happening without excusing harmful behaviour: 'My alarm is high. I feel angry. My goal is a safe bedtime.' They lower their voice and offer two acceptable choices: pyjamas first or teeth first.
Name it, then return to the goal
Three circles overlap into one integrated response.
Integration means the parent uses protection for safety, emotion for connection and thinking for a plan. All three have a role. None should run the whole interaction alone.
Safety + connection + plan
Prompt card.
Ask yourself: What is my alarm saying? What feeling is present? What is my parenting goal?
Alarm - feeling - goal
after_video: Why is the three-part brain described as a teaching model rather than literal anatomy?
What did the parent assume when protective and emotional processes took over?
How did naming the parenting goal help the parent respond?

activities.title: Activity 2 - Bring Thinking Back

lessons.title: Fight, Flight, Freeze and Fawn - Recognising Your Survival Responses
lessons.overview: Stress responses can appear as confrontation, escape, shutdown or appeasing. Fight, flight and freeze are common shorthand for threat responses. 'Fawn' is used here as a trauma-informed description of automatic appeasing or over-agreeing; it is not a formal diagnosis or a universal biological category.
objectives: recognise fight, flight, freeze and appeasing patterns
identify both obvious and quiet forms of survival responding
separate automatic responses from intentional parenting values
notice what each pattern protects against
choose a safer response for one common trigger
lessons.definition_prompt: When you hear fight, flight, freeze and fawn, what behaviours or body sensations come to mind?
checkin: I become louder, controlling, argumentative or physically tense.
I leave, avoid, distract myself or want the situation to end immediately.
I go blank, become numb or cannot decide what to do.
I agree, give in or apologise automatically to stop conflict.
My response changes depending on the person or situation.
key_points: Fight
May look like yelling, arguing, threatening, controlling, blaming or preparing to confront.
Flight
May look like leaving, avoiding, overworking, changing the subject, using a phone or substance, or ending contact abruptly.
Freeze
May look like going blank, becoming still, feeling numb, losing words or delaying necessary action.
Fawn or automatic appeasing
May look like saying yes, over-apologising, abandoning a boundary or taking responsibility for everything to reduce conflict.
Responsibility without shame
An automatic response can be understandable and still require change when it harms safety, connection or consistency.
lessons.video_goal: Demonstrate four versions of the same child refusal and show the regulated alternative.
video_scenes: Title cards for fight, flight, freeze and appease with body silhouettes.
When the nervous system detects threat, people may confront, escape, become still or try to keep the other person pleased. These patterns can be fast and automatic.
Survival patterns
Child refuses to turn off a game. Fight version: parent raises voice, moves close and threatens an extreme punishment.
Fight can look like pressure, argument or control. The body may feel hot, strong and ready to act. The protective purpose is often to stop the threat or regain control.
Fight: confront or control
Flight version: parent walks away, says 'Do whatever you want,' and avoids returning to the issue.

Flight can look like leaving physically or emotionally. The protective purpose is to escape discomfort, conflict or fear. Leaving for safety can be appropriate; abandoning necessary supervision or follow-through is different.
Flight: escape or avoid
Freeze version: parent stares, cannot answer, then lets the situation continue without a decision.

Freeze can look like silence, numbness or losing access to words. The protective purpose is to become still until danger passes. A freeze response is not laziness, but it can prevent timely protective action.
Freeze: still, blank or numb
Appease version: parent immediately says the child can keep playing and then apologises for setting the limit.
Automatic appeasing, sometimes called fawning, can look like giving in, over-apologising or abandoning your own limit so the conflict stops. This term is a trauma-informed shorthand, not a diagnosis.
Appease: keep peace at any cost
Regulated version. Parent steps back, names body signal, states limit and two choices, then follows through.

A safer response begins with recognition: 'I want to yell or give in.' The parent creates space and says, 'Game time is finished. You can save now or I will help turn it off. You can be upset, and the limit stays.'
Recognise - regulate - respond
Four arrows point to needs: control, escape, stillness, approval. Then arrows point to skills.
Each pattern tries to protect something. Change becomes possible when you identify the pattern, understand its protective purpose and practise a response that protects safety without repeating harm.
Understand the protection; change the action
Prompt card.
Which pattern appears first for you? What does it try to protect you from?
My pattern - my protection - my safer choice
after_video: How did each survival pattern change the parent's follow-through?
Which responses were quieter and therefore easier to miss?
What was different about the regulated response?

lessons.title: What Triggers Mean and Where They Come From
lessons.overview: A trigger is a cue that activates a strong emotional, body or behavioural response because it is linked with threat, loss, shame, helplessness or earlier experience. Triggers explain intensity; they do not automatically prove current danger or excuse harmful action.
objectives: define a trigger without using it as an excuse
distinguish the present event from the meaning attached to it
identify common sensory, relational and situational cues
check whether the current situation requires protection or regulation
create a trigger-response plan
lessons.definition_prompt: What does the word trigger mean to you? How is a trigger different from a deliberate choice or a current danger?
checkin: Certain tones of voice affect me more strongly than the words themselves.
Being ignored, criticised or challenged creates a strong reaction.
Mess, noise, lateness or unpredictability can make me feel unsafe or out of control.

I can identify experiences that may have shaped some of my triggers.
key_points: Trigger cue
A sound, expression, smell, body sensation, situation, topic or relationship pattern can activate an alarm response.
Attached meaning
The mind may rapidly interpret the cue as rejection, danger, humiliation, abandonment or loss of control.
Past and present
Earlier experiences can shape sensitivity, but current stress, sleep, pain and pressure also affect reactions.
Check the facts
Ask what is happening now, whether anyone is in immediate danger and what information is still missing.
Respond, do not excuse
A trigger can explain intensity. The parent remains responsible for safety, words, actions and repair.

lessons.title: How Your Nervous System Affects Your Children
lessons.overview: Children continually read adult cues such as voice, face, movement, availability and predictability. A parent's state does not determine every child response, but it can add threat, offer safety or shape the speed of recovery. The lesson focuses on responsibility without blaming parents for all child distress.
objectives: identify the adult cues children notice
explain how escalation can become reciprocal
distinguish influence from total responsibility
practise calm, firm co-regulatory signals
plan repair after a dysregulated interaction
lessons.definition_prompt: How do you think a child can tell whether an adult feels calm, angry, frightened, distracted or unavailable?
checkin: My child notices changes in my voice before I do.
When I move quickly or speak sharply, my child may become louder or more withdrawn.
I can stay emotionally available while maintaining a safety limit.
I sometimes expect my child to calm before I change my own approach.
I know how to repair after I have frightened, shamed or disconnected from my child.
key_points: Children read non-verbal cues
Tone, pace, facial expression, distance, posture and predictability may communicate safety or threat.
Stress can become reciprocal
A child's distress activates the parent; the parent's activation can then increase the child's distress.
Influence is not total control
Parents influence the interaction, but children also have temperament, development, neurodiversity, experiences and needs.
Calm and firm
Regulation is compatible with supervision, consequences and clear limits.
Repair changes the pattern
A specific apology, reassurance of safety and changed follow-through can restore connection.
lessons.video_goal: Show an escalation loop, a co-regulated version and a repair sequence.
video_scenes: Child watches adult face, voice waveform and body movement.
Children gather information from more than words. They watch adult faces, volume, speed, distance and whether the adult remains predictable.
Children read the whole interaction
Escalation loop: child whines, parent tenses, voice rises, child screams, parent moves closer.

Stress can travel back and forth. The child's distress activates the parent. The parent's louder voice and faster movement add threat. The child becomes more distressed, which activates the parent further.
The escalation loop
Pause overlay. Parent steps to safe distance, lowers volume, uses fewer words.
The parent cannot control every child reaction, but can change the signals they contribute. They slow down, use fewer words and keep their body at a respectful distance.
Change the signals you add
Parent: 'I will not let you hit. I am moving the chair back. I am here when your hands are safe.'
Co-regulation is not letting unsafe behaviour continue. The adult blocks or reduces danger, names the limit and remains emotionally available.
Safety and connection together
Child remains upset but intensity gradually lowers. Parent waits before teaching.
The aim is not instant compliance. The first task may be safety and recovery. Teaching, problem-solving and consequences work better when both people can process language.
Regulate before teaching
Repair scene later. Parent kneels at respectful distance.
If the parent yelled, repair should be specific: 'I shouted and moved too close. That was frightening. Your hitting still was not safe. Next time I will step back and use a quieter voice.'
Repair without removing the limit
Four cue icons.
Ask: What is my face saying? What is my voice saying? What is my body saying? Is my behaviour predictable?
Face - voice - body - predictability

lessons.title: Window of Tolerance - Finding and Expanding Your Calm Zone
lessons.overview: The 'window of tolerance' is a useful clinical metaphor for the range of activation in which a person can remain present, think flexibly and act according to goals. Above the window may involve high activation; below it may involve shutdown. It is not a diagnostic test and the boundaries change with context.
objectives: use the window metaphor carefully
identify regulated, high-activation and low-activation states
match strategies to the current state
recognise factors that narrow or widen capacity
plan regular practice rather than crisis-only use
lessons.definition_prompt: What does being inside, above or below your calm zone mean to you?
checkin: I can recognise when I am still able to listen and think.
I notice when I become too activated to problem-solve.
I notice low-energy shutdown, numbness or disconnection.
My capacity changes with sleep, stress, pain and support.
I practise regulation skills before I reach crisis level.
key_points: Inside the workable zone
You can feel emotion while staying present, using language and choosing actions.
Above the zone
High activation may include racing thoughts, panic, anger, urgency, agitation or sensory overload.
Below the zone
Low activation may include numbness, heaviness, disconnection, collapse or difficulty initiating action.
The zone changes
Sleep, illness, trauma reminders, conflict, substance use, workload and support can narrow or widen capacity.
Match the tool
High activation may need slowing and grounding; low activation may need orientation, movement, light and connection.
lessons.video_goal: Animate a flexible zone meter and demonstrate different tools for high and low activation.
video_scenes: A vertical meter with a flexible green middle band, orange upper band and blue lower band.
The window of tolerance is a practical metaphor for the range in which you can stay present, think and act according to your goals. It is not a test or fixed personality trait.
A flexible working zone
Parent in green zone handling a child complaint while breathing steadily.
Inside the workable zone, you may still feel annoyed, sad or worried. Regulation does not mean no emotion. It means enough access to language, perspective and choice.
Emotion with choice
Meter rises. Parent paces, speaks rapidly and sees threat-focused thought bubbles.
Above the zone, activation may become intense. The body prepares for action. You may feel urgent, angry, panicked or unable to tolerate noise and delay.
Above: high activation
Meter drops. Parent looks distant, heavy and slow, with muffled sound.
Below the zone, the system may conserve energy or disconnect. You may feel numb, collapsed, unreal, unable to speak or unable to begin a necessary task.
Below: shutdown or low activation
Two toolkits. High: feet, longer exhale, reduce stimulation. Low: orient to room, stand, stretch, cold water, contact support.

Different states may need different tools. High activation often benefits from slowing, reducing stimulation and grounding. Low activation may benefit from gentle movement, sensory orientation and safe connection.
Match the tool to the state
Band narrows during sleep deprivation and widens with routine practice and support.
Capacity changes. Poor sleep, pain, conflict and accumulated stress can narrow the window. Predictable routines, support, regular practice and reduced stressors can widen usable capacity.
Context changes capacity
Parent fills a three-zone plan.
Your task is to recognise your zone earlier and choose a matched action. You do not need to diagnose yourself; you need a practical map.
Recognise - match - practise

lessons.title: Early Warning Signs - Noticing Before You React
lessons.overview: Early warning signs are the first observable changes in body, attention, thoughts, voice or urges. The lesson teaches a traffic-light system so parents can act at yellow rather than waiting for red.
objectives: separate green, yellow and red signs
identify the first change in voice, body or thinking
create a yellow-light intervention
plan how another safe adult can provide feedback
measure progress by earlier noticing, not perfection
lessons.definition_prompt: What is the first sign that tells you a difficult parenting moment may be escalating?
checkin: I notice changes in my thoughts before my behaviour changes.
I notice changes in my voice before I yell or shut down.
I have a yellow-light plan for early activation.
I can receive feedback from a safe person without treating it as an attack.
I measure progress by noticing earlier and recovering sooner.
key_points: Green
Available, connected and able to think. This is the best time to practise skills and plan.
Yellow
Early activation: tension, repetition, urgency, sharper tone, reduced listening or urge to control/escape.
Red
High activation or shutdown: unsafe behaviour, loss of language, panic, rage, collapse or inability to supervise effectively.
Act at yellow
Reduce words, slow movement, check safety and use the planned tool before the interaction reaches red.
Progress markers
Earlier notice, shorter escalation, less harm, faster repair and more consistent follow-through.
lessons.video_goal: Replay an escalation in slow motion, identifying the exact yellow-light point.
video_scenes: Traffic-light graphic with green, yellow and red descriptions.
Most reactions do not begin at maximum intensity. There is often a yellow-light period when small changes appear in the body, thoughts, voice or urges.
Act before red
Normal-speed scene of morning conflict ending in yelling.
At normal speed, escalation can feel sudden. The parent repeats an instruction, the child argues, the parent yells and both people become overwhelmed.
Escalation can feel instant
Scene replays slowly. Markers appear: breath held, jaw tight, thought 'They are doing this on purpose,' voice becomes clipped.

In slow motion, the early signs are visible. The parent holds their breath. Their jaw tightens. They repeat the same sentence. Their thinking becomes certain and their voice becomes sharper. This is yellow.
Find the first change
At yellow, parent uses prepared phrase and timer: 'I am getting stressed. Shoes still need to go on. I am taking three breaths, then I will help.'
A yellow-light plan should be short enough to use under pressure. Reduce words, slow movement, keep supervision and use the regulation action you practised while calm.
Use a prepared yellow plan
Trusted adult gently says 'yellow' in another scene; parent nods and steps back.
Some parents use a neutral cue from a safe adult. The cue must never be used to shame, control or provoke. Agree in advance what the cue means and what action follows.
Safe feedback can help
Progress chart: notice at red, then late yellow, then early yellow.
Progress may look like noticing at red, then later noticing at yellow, then eventually acting at the first signal. Recovery time and repair also matter.
Measure earlier notice
Prompt card.
What is your first yellow sign? What is your automatic next step?
My yellow sign - my next step

Why was the prepared phrase short?
How can a support person's cue be used safely rather than critically?

lessons.title: Grounding Techniques - Bringing Yourself Back to the Present
lessons.overview: Grounding directs attention to present sensory information, location, time and immediate safety. It may help when a person feels overwhelmed, disconnected or caught in trigger-based thinking. Not every grounding method suits every person; tools should be tested while calm and stopped if they increase distress.
objectives: explain the purpose of grounding
practise sensory, orientation and pressure-based grounding
choose methods compatible with child supervision
recognise when a technique is unhelpful
create a portable grounding card
lessons.definition_prompt: What does 'bringing yourself back to the present' mean to you?
checkin: When overwhelmed, I lose awareness of the room or current time.
I become stuck in memories, feared outcomes or repetitive thoughts.
Focusing on my senses can sometimes help me orient.
Some breathing or body exercises make me more uncomfortable.
I have grounding options that allow me to keep supervising my child.
key_points: Present orientation
Grounding uses current facts: name, date, location, people present and immediate safety.
Sensory attention
Sight, sound, touch, smell and taste can anchor attention in the current environment.
Pressure and contact
Feet on the floor, hands together, wall pressure or holding a textured object may provide clear body information.
Choice and consent
Grounding should not be forced. Stop or switch if a method increases panic, pain, dizziness or disconnection.
Safety first
Grounding is not a substitute for leaving immediate danger, seeking emergency help or obtaining clinical care.
lessons.video_goal: Lead the viewer through three grounding options with accessible alternatives.
video_scenes: Presenter seated with feet visible and a clear, uncluttered background.

Grounding means directing attention to what is happening here and now. It can be useful when stress pulls attention into memories, feared outcomes, panic or disconnection. Keep your eyes open if that feels safer.
Grounding: here, now, safe enough
Orientation card appears.

Option one is orientation. Say your name, where you are, the date or time of day, who is present and the next safe task. For example: 'I am in my kitchen. It is Monday morning. My children are here. No one is injured. The next task is to move the broken glass.'
Name - place - time - people - next task
Presenter completes a shortened 5-4-3-2-1 exercise.

Option two is sensory grounding. Name five things you see, four things you can feel, three sounds, two smells and one taste. You can shorten this. Do not force a sense that is uncomfortable or unavailable.
Use the senses flexibly
Feet press, hands press, wall press; seated alternative shown.

Option three is pressure and contact. Press both feet into the floor for five seconds and release. Press your palms together. If safe, push gently into a wall. Notice pressure, temperature and contact. Avoid pain or breath-holding.
Pressure without pain
Parent uses grounding while child is upset nearby; child remains in view.

A parenting grounding tool must preserve supervision. Keep the child in view, use few words and choose a tool that does not require leaving a young child alone or closing your eyes if that reduces safety.
Ground while supervising
Alternative card: look for colours, alphabet objects, hold cool cloth, describe object.

If one method is unhelpful, try another: find five blue objects, name items from A to E, describe a textured object or place a cool cloth on your hands. Some people find breath-focused exercises uncomfortable, so use choice.
One tool does not fit everyone
Stop/seek help icons.
Stop if the technique increases distress, pain, dizziness or disconnection. Grounding supports present awareness; it does not replace emergency action, medical care or trauma treatment.
Stop, switch or seek support
after_video: Which grounding option required the least interruption to supervision?
What adaptations were offered for people who dislike breath focus or closing their eyes?
When is grounding not the first priority?

lessons.title: Breathing and Body-Based Regulation Tools
lessons.overview: Breathing and body-based tools can help create a relaxation response or increase body awareness. They should be gentle, never forced and adapted for health conditions, pregnancy, pain, dizziness or trauma-related discomfort. Some people prefer movement or muscle-release methods rather than breath focus.
objectives: practise gentle paced breathing without forcing depth
use longer-exhale and muscle-release options
identify alternatives to breath-focused exercises
match tools to activation level and supervision needs
create a two-tool practice routine
lessons.definition_prompt: Which breathing, movement or muscle-release methods have helped or not helped you in the past?
checkin: I tend to hold my breath or breathe rapidly when stressed.
Slow breathing is comfortable for me.
Focusing on breathing can make me dizzy, panicked or self-conscious.
Gentle movement or muscle release is more useful for me.
I practise body tools while calm rather than waiting for crisis.
key_points: Gentle, not forced
Let the breath move comfortably; forcing very deep breaths can increase discomfort or dizziness.
Longer exhale
A slightly longer, easy out-breath may support settling for some people.
Muscle release
Jaw, shoulders, hands and feet can be tensed gently and released without pain.
Movement options
Walking, stretching, shaking out hands, wall pressure or rhythmic movement may help regulate.
Health adaptation
Seek professional advice when symptoms, medical conditions or trauma responses make an exercise unsafe or distressing.
lessons.video_goal: Guide four options: paced breathing, longer exhale, release, and movement, with opt-out language.
video_scenes: Presenter seated and standing options. Disclaimer card.

Body-based tools are experiments, not tests. Choose a comfortable position. Do not force deep breathing. Stop if you feel pain, severe dizziness, faintness or increased panic, and use appropriate medical support when needed.
Comfort first - never force
Animated circle expands and contracts gently for equal breathing.
Option one is gentle paced breathing. Let the breath come in comfortably, then flow out comfortably. You may count three in and three out. The goal is regularity, not the biggest possible breath.
Gentle 3 in - 3 out
Rectangle animation: shorter inhale, slightly longer exhale, no hold.
Option two is a longer exhale. Breathe in gently for three and out for four or five, only if comfortable. There is no need to hold the breath. Return to normal breathing at any time.

lessons.title: Co-Regulation - How Calm Parents Create Calm Children
lessons.overview: Co-regulation is the supportive process through which a caring adult provides a warm relationship, coaching and a structured environment that helps a child build self-regulation. A parent does not need to be perfectly calm; they need to reduce threat, preserve safety and offer predictable support.
objectives: define co-regulation accurately
model calm voice, pace, posture and concise language
maintain safety limits during emotional distress
delay teaching until the child can process
repair when the parent becomes dysregulated
lessons.definition_prompt: What does co-regulation mean to you? How is it different from giving in or making a child stop feeling upset?
checkin: I can remain nearby without crowding my child.
I can use fewer words when my child is overwhelmed.
I can validate emotion without approving unsafe behaviour.
I can keep a limit steady even when my child is angry.
I know how to repair when I add to the escalation.
key_points: Warm relationship
The adult communicates availability, respect and interest.
Coaching and modelling
The adult demonstrates regulation and helps the child name feelings, body signs and strategies.
Structured environment
Predictable limits, routines and reduced hazards support regulation.
Safety before teaching
During intense distress, use short language and protective action; teach later.
Development and difference
Co-regulation should match age, communication ability, culture, neurodiversity and sensory needs.
lessons.video_goal: Model co-regulation during a hitting incident, including safety, validation, recovery and later teaching.
video_scenes: Adult and child connected by a gentle animated line; three pillars appear.
Co-regulation is the process through which a caring adult provides a supportive relationship, coaching and a structured environment that helps a child develop self-regulation.
Relationship - coaching - structure
Child becomes overwhelmed and raises a hand. Parent steps between children and moves a hard object.
Co-regulation starts with safety. The parent blocks hitting, creates space and removes hazards. They do not wait for the child to agree before protecting people.
Protect first
Parent at respectful distance, low voice: 'I will not let you hit. Your body is very upset. I am here.'
The parent uses a low, steady voice and few words: 'I will not let you hit. Your body is very upset. I am here.' The feeling is acknowledged. The unsafe action is still stopped.
Validate feeling; stop unsafe action
Parent offers two regulation choices: sit nearby or hold cushion; child rejects both. Parent remains steady.
Co-regulation offers support without demanding instant calm. The child may refuse a strategy. The adult can remain predictable and repeat the safety message without arguing.
Offer, do not force
Child's body settles. Parent waits, gets water and reconnects.
Recovery may take time. The adult watches breathing, movement and ability to hear language. The aim is not to win the argument; it is to restore enough safety and connection for learning.
Watch for readiness
Later conversation: parent and child identify trigger, repair object and practise words.

Teaching happens later: what happened, what feeling was present, what action was unsafe, what can be done next time and what repair is needed. Consequences should be related, proportionate and understandable.
Teach and repair later
Adult repair version: 'I shouted. That added fear. I am sorry. The hitting rule still stands.'
Parents also need repair. 'I shouted and that added fear. I am sorry. The hitting rule still stands. Next time I will step back and use fewer words.'
Adult accountability supports safety
Age/diversity adaptation icons.
Adapt the approach for age, disability, language, sensory needs, culture and the child's history. Co-regulation is responsive, not one fixed script.
Responsive, not one-size-fits-all

lessons.title: Building My Personal Regulation Plan - Putting It All Together
lessons.overview: The final lesson combines triggers, body signals, zones, grounding, body tools, co-regulation, support and repair into a personalised plan. The plan must include immediate safety actions and escalation pathways, not only calming techniques.
objectives: combine learning from the full course
identify predictable triggers and early signs
select matched tools and co-regulation scripts
define when to step away, seek support or use emergency action
create a measurable practice and evidence plan
lessons.definition_prompt: What would a useful personal regulation plan need to include so that it works during real parenting pressure?
checkin: I know my most common triggers and survival patterns.
I know my early yellow signs and red-level risks.
I have tools for both high activation and shutdown.
I have a plan for maintaining child supervision and immediate safety.
I know who to contact when self-regulation is not enough.
key_points: Before stress
Reduce predictable pressures, practise tools, prepare routines and tell support people what helps.
At yellow
Use the earliest signal, brief pause, matched tool and short parenting script.
At red
Prioritise child safety, reduce access to hazards, involve a safe adult and follow crisis/emergency procedures.
Afterwards
Repair, review what worked, update the plan and document repeated practice.
Evidence of change
Look for earlier notice, safer behaviour, consistent follow-through, faster recovery and honest repair over time.
lessons.video_goal: Build a complete plan on screen using a realistic family example and clear safety escalation points.
video_scenes: Blank plan with sections: triggers, signs, tools, safety, support, repair, evidence.
A regulation plan turns insight into a sequence that can be used under pressure. It must be short enough to follow and detailed enough to protect children when stress becomes high.
A plan for real pressure
Trigger section fills: noise during school rush, feeling ignored, contact with stressful services.
Start with predictable triggers and contexts. Include events, meanings and conditions that narrow capacity, such as poor sleep, conflict, pain, deadlines or substance use.
Know the pressure points
Signs section fills with green/yellow/red.
List your early yellow signs and red-level risks. Be specific: jaw tight, repeating instructions, urge to grab a phone, leaving without telling anyone, going blank or losing supervision.
Specific signs guide action
Matched tools fill: high activation and low activation.

Choose tools that match your state. High activation may need slowing, grounding and space. Shutdown may need orientation, movement and contact with a safe person. Include a backup when the first tool fails.
Primary and backup tools
Safety plan fills: move children from hazard, hand supervision to approved adult, do not drive, secure dangerous items, call support.

A complete plan is more than calming. State exactly how children will remain supervised, how hazards will be reduced and what actions are prohibited when you are highly activated, such as driving, threatening or leaving young children alone.
Safety actions are non-negotiable
Support ladder: self-tool, trusted adult, professional, crisis/emergency.

Create a support ladder. Who can provide practical help? Which professional service is appropriate? When does the situation require urgent or emergency action? Use local professional advice to complete these contacts.
Know when self-help is not enough
Co-regulation and repair scripts fill in.
Add words you can use: a yellow-light sentence, a safety limit, a co-regulation phrase and a repair statement. Prepared language reduces the need to invent words while stressed.
Prepare the words
Evidence tracker shows repeated entries over weeks.

Measure change over time: earlier noticing, reduced intensity, safer choices, consistent limits, shorter recovery and completed repair. One good day or one difficult day should not define the whole pattern.
Evidence is repeated behaviour
Plan is printed and saved privately.
Review the plan with an appropriate professional or support person, store it where it can be accessed safely and update it after practice.
Practise - review - update

Why does the plan include both primary and backup tools?
What evidence would show meaningful change over time?
